nameStory: The "moonwort" name comes from the crescent-shaped segments of this fern's fertile frond, which early botanists thought resembled phases of the moon. The "swamp" part refers to its love of wet, boggy places. Medieval herbalists believed moonworts had magical properties and could unlock doors when picked under a full moon!
description: Swamp moonwort is a tiny, unusual fern that looks more like a miniature flowering plant than what most people expect from a fern. It grows only 2-6 inches tall and has a unique two-part structure: one small, fan-shaped sterile frond that does the photosynthesis work, and one separate fertile stalk that holds the spores in grape-like clusters. **[Uncertain claim flagged: exact size range and detailed morphology]** This diminutive plant is easily overlooked among the grasses and sedges of its wetland home.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Has two distinct parts: a small, fan-shaped sterile frond with wedge-shaped segments, and a separate fertile stalk with tiny bead-like clusters that feel firm when fresh

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Extremely small at 2-6 inches tall, growing singly rather than in clumps, often hidden among other wetland plants

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Single smooth stem that splits into the two frond parts, feeling succulent and slightly fleshy rather than wiry like most ferns

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spores contained in rounded, bead-like structures clustered on the fertile stalk, turning from green to brownish as they mature

habitat: **[Uncertain claim flagged: specific habitat requirements]** Found in wet, acidic soils of swamps, bogs, and marshy areas throughout New England's lowlands. Often grows among sphagnum moss, sedges, and other bog plants in areas that stay consistently moist. Prefers partially shaded spots rather than full sun exposure.

seasonality.spring: Tiny fronds emerge directly from the ground in late spring, already showing their distinctive two-part structure without the typical fern fiddleheads.
seasonality.summer: Both sterile and fertile fronds are fully developed and easiest to spot, with the fertile stalk showing green spore clusters that gradually mature.
seasonality.fall: Spores ripen to brown and are released, while the entire plant begins to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, existing only as underground gametophytes and roots.

funFact: This tiny fern is so rare and secretive that it was only scientifically described in 1979, making it one of the most recently discovered ferns in North America - there are probably individual oak trees older than our knowledge of this species!
confusionNotes: **[Uncertain claim flagged: specific confusion species]** Most likely confused with other tiny moonworts or even small seedling plants rather than typical ferns. The key is looking for that unique two-part structure - one leafy part and one beaded fertile stalk from the same base. If it looks like a normal fern, even a small one, it's probably something else.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called moonworts, these plants are true ferns that reproduce by spores, not seeds like flowering plants. The Botrychium genus is ancient and quite different from typical ferns - they don't even form the classic coiled fiddleheads that most ferns are known for.
compareHints: **[Uncertain claim flagged: specific comparison details]** Swamp moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for wet habitats and its small, fan-shaped sterile frond segments. Other moonworts like little grapefern tend to prefer drier soils, while matricary grapefern has more finely divided, lacy frond segments rather than the simple wedge shapes of swamp moonwort.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Matricary grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its chamomile-like leaf segments that are more finely divided than most of its relatives.
Narrow triangle moonwort differs from matricary grapefern by having much narrower, more pointed segments rather than finely dissected, lacy ones.
Little grapefern is distinguished from other moonworts by its simple, often undivided leaf blade, whereas matricary grapefern and others have multiple leaflets or more complex divisions.

Upswept moonwort differs from other moonworts by its fan or wedge-shaped leaflet segments that angle upward, rather than the more rounded or deeply divided segments of relatives like matricary grapefern.
Unlike its moonwort relatives with their more typical triangular or oval leaflet shapes, spathulate moonwort's spatula-shaped segments are unmistakable.
Prairie moonwort is distinguished from other moonworts by its preference for dry, prairie-like conditions rather than the moist, shaded habitats preferred by most of its relatives.
